core: Blues as an African American secular musical genre
Historical roots in the rural U.S. South
The 12-bar and AAB patterns as common but non-universal conventions
Careful listening to repeated lines, harmonic movement, pitch inflection, and performance context
supporting: Early recordings and urban as well as rural blues
The genre's influence on later U.S. popular music
Differences among individual artists, settings, and blues styles

claims.claim: Blues is a secular African American musical genre with roots in the rural American South at the end of the nineteenth century, and it gained wider momentum early in the twentieth century.
Blues deals with varied subjects and emotions; it should not be reduced to songs only about sorrow or protest.
The 12-bar blues and an AAB lyric pattern are common conventions, but the word blues can also describe music that does not follow that exact form.
A common 12-bar blues harmonic model uses the tonic, subdominant, and dominant functions, often described with the Roman numerals I, IV, and V.
Early recorded country blues often featured a singer accompanying themself on acoustic guitar, while blues was also performed with other instruments and in social dance settings.
By the 1920s, blues was also being recorded and popularized in urban settings, and later electric blues and rhythm and blues helped shape subsequent popular-music histories.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether the 12-bar form, AAB text pattern, blue notes, or a sad mood defines all blues music.
positions: Introductory accounts commonly teach a 12-bar I-IV-V form and AAB lyric design.
The word blues is also used more broadly, and performances vary in form, text, instrumentation, setting, and affect.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: Teach the common convention as a listening tool and explicitly reject it as a universal test for the genre.

unsupportedExistingClaims: The generated draft was generic placeholder material and did not substantively define the blues, explain its African American history, or distinguish a common form from the whole genre.
correctionsNeeded: Replaced placeholder prose with source-verified history and musical vocabulary.

Qualified the 12-bar and AAB models as common conventions rather than mandatory rules.
